orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the December 17, 2019 order granting summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion and dismissed the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped and fell on a snow-covered piece of debris on defendant’s property. The opinion does not identify the debris, the specific fall location, or the property’s use.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant did not establish relinquishment of control sufficient to extinguish the premises-maintenance duty as a matter of law.
Defendant failed to establish noncreation; pointing to gaps in plaintiff’s proof did not satisfy defendant’s initial burden.
Defendant failed to establish lack of actual notice; plaintiff’s alleged failure of proof did not substitute for the required initial showing.
Defendant failed to establish lack of constructive notice; the court did not find notice conclusively established.

evidence_discussed.description: Moving papers asserted deficiencies in plaintiff’s proof; no specific testimony, documents or other evidentiary format is identified, and relinquishment-of-control evidence was not supplied.

quality.notes: Actual fall site is expressly defendant’s property; the court also addresses his unextinguished maintenance duty. Private control is recorded without inferring title, premises use, accident date or plaintiff’s role. Failure to show relinquishment is not an affirmative finding of an ownership interest or landlord relationship. Snow-covered debris does not establish a storm defense. Initial-burden failure is not proven creation or notice. Apply unchanged rules to this preliminary validation-period case.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously reversed on the law without costs, the motion is denied and the complaint is reinstated.
Memorandum: Plaintiff commenced this action seeking to recover damages for injuries that he sustained when he slipped and fell on a snow-covered piece of debris on defendant's property.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Erie County (Paul Wojtaszek, J.), entered December 17, 2019. The order granted the motion of defendant for summary judgment and dismissed the complaint.
Here, defendant failed to establish that he did not create the dangerous condition and did not have actual or constructive notice of that condition

Defendant's assertion in his moving papers that plaintiff failed to demonstrate that defendant created or had notice of the dangerous condition is insufficient to establish a prima facie case that defendant is not liable as a matter of law
Furthermore, defendant did not submit evidence establishing that he relinquished control over the property such that his duty to maintain the premises was extinguished as a matter of law
We agree with plaintiff that defendant failed to meet his initial burden on his motion, and thus the court was required to deny the motion "regardless of the sufficiency of the opposing papers"
Plaintiff appeals, and we reverse.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the December 1, 2014 order granting summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: After shopping at defendants’ store on December 15, 2011, plaintiff allegedly slipped on an oil patch in the parking lot.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants offered no evidence of when the fall area was last inspected or cleaned, so they failed their initial lack-of-constructive-notice showing regardless of the opposition.

quality.notes: Store attribution and a fall in the parking lot do not explicitly establish ownership, lease or private control of that lot. General owner/possessor rules and a failed notice showing do not supply the missing property relationship. Retail describes the associated shopping setting, not an ownership conclusion. Oil is preserved in the summary and coded other rather than assuming water or grease composition. Customer role and complete accident date are explicit. No specific evidence format or inspection records are identified; the evidence list is empty, not a finding that litigation had no evidence. Creation, actual notice and duty occur only in the general legal test, without separately analyzed case-specific grounds.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.
On December 15, 2011, the plaintiff had just finished shopping at the defendants' store when she allegedly slipped and fell on an oil patch in the parking lot.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Kitzes, J.), entered December 1, 2014, which granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

In support of their motion, the defendants failed to demonstrate, prima facie, a lack of constructive notice of the allegedly hazardous condition that caused the subject accident, as they failed to submit any evidence as to when, prior to the accident, the area of the parking lot where the alleged slip and fall occurred, was last inspected or cleaned relative to the accident

Since the defendants failed to demonstrate their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the Supreme Court should have denied their motion without regard to the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the December 17, 2010 denial of summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell while exiting his apartment building when the exterior doormat shifted beneath his right foot. He described longstanding upturned corners and frequent shifting that required him to reposition the mat.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant asserted noncreation, but the court’s specific grounds were constructive-notice and hazard-proof deficiencies rather than a separate determination of creation.
Defendant asserted lack of actual notice; the opinion specifically resolves constructive-notice and hazard showings without separately deciding actual knowledge.
Defendant provided no last-inspection evidence; the superintendent’s last walk over the mat did not establish an inspection. Defendant therefore failed to establish lack of constructive notice.
Defendant failed to establish that the allegedly shifting, curled-corner mat was not hazardous; no final hazard or negligence finding was made.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted plaintiff’s deposition describing the mat’s longstanding upturned corners and repeated movement.
The opinion distinguishes evidence of the superintendent walking over the mat from evidence of an inspection, without identifying the format of the superintendent account.

quality.notes: Express apartment-building ownership and the mat’s location on those premises support private property. “His apartment building” supports residence but not a specific tenant/owner/guest relationship, so injured role remains unclear. Accident date is unstated. Other captures the shifting mat and obstruction captures its raised corners; no trip mechanism is substituted for the stated slip. Frequent shifting is testimony considered in the notice/hazard discussion, not an express separate recurring-condition doctrine or proof defendant knew about it. The superintendent’s walk is not equated with inspection, and no testimony format is invented for that account.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, without costs or disbursements.
The plaintiff, while in the process of exiting his apartment building, which was owned by the defendant, allegedly slipped and fell on a mat situated outside the door to the building.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Dutchess County (Brands, J.), dated December 17, 2010, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

At his deposition, the plaintiff testified that, after he stepped on the mat with his right foot, the mat, which had been located in *803 the same position for “[y]ears,” moved, causing him to lose his balance and fall.

According to the plaintiffs deposition testimony, submitted by the defendant in support of its motion, all four of the corners of the mat, which had been on the premises for “a very long time,” were turned up, and the mat would frequently move out of its position when he would step on it, causing him to have to reposition it.

Since the defendant offered no evidence as to when the mat was last inspected prior to the accident, as opposed to the last time its superintendent walked over it, the defendant failed to make a prima facie showing that it did not have constructive notice of the alleged defective condition of the mat
Moreover, contrary to the defendant’s contention, it failed to establish, prima facie, that the condition which allegedly caused the plaintiff’s accident was not hazardous

In view of the defendant’s failure to meet its prima facie burden, its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint was properly denied, and we need not review the sufficiency of the plaintiff’s opposition papers
The defendant moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the ground, inter alia, that it neither created nor had actual or constructive notice of the alleged hazardous condition.
The defendant appeals, and we affirm.

orders.description: Defendants’ limited appeal from the August 31, 2012 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as appealed from.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on urine on stairs in a building owned and/or managed by defendants. Plaintiff and witnesses described persistent urine and debris; a tenant described the condition at the fall site hours earlier and prior complaints, while the porter described regular cleaning and no accident-day urine observations or complaints.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants’ submissions raised triable issues of a visible, apparent condition present long enough to remedy; specific earlier observations and disputed cleaning practices prevented summary judgment.

The court found a triable issue of constructive notice of an ongoing, recurring condition routinely left unaddressed, supported by testimony of frequent urine/debris, earlier complaints and prior slips.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff described persistent urine/debris and smelling urine nearly two hours before the fall, though he had not seen it before slipping.
Porter described daily cleaning and no accident-day notice; nonparty witnesses disputed cleaning regularity and described earlier urine, complaints and prior slips.

quality.notes: Express owned/managed premises, tenant references and porter responsibilities support private residential control. Owned and/or managed are collective alternatives, not a finding every defendant held both roles. Plaintiff’s own tenancy and accident date are unstated. Other preserves urine as distinct from water; debris is also described. Testimony about complaints is recorded, but the court’s articulated notice analysis is constructive/recurring, not a separate actual-notice finding. Conflicting cleaning accounts and earlier timing remain unresolved; no liability or specific dangerous-condition creation is found. The entire appealed scope is affirmed.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (John A. Barone, J.), entered August 31, 2012, which, in this action arising from plaintiff Raymond Hill’s alleged slip and fall on stairs in a building owned and/or managed by defendants, to the extent appealed from, denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.

Defendants’ submissions raise triable issues of fact as to whether they had constructive notice of a visible and apparent dangerous condition that existed for a sufficient length of time before the accident to permit them to discover and remedy it
and whether they had constructive notice of an ongoing and recurring dangerous condition existing in the area of the accident that they routinely left unaddressed

Indeed, defendants’ porter averred that he followed a daily routine in which he inspected and cleaned the hallways and stairwells in the morning, that he would respond to any complaints throughout the day until the end of his shift at 5:00 p.m., and that he did not observe or receive any complaints of urine in the stairwell on the date of the accident.

However, *643 plaintiff and two nonparty witnesses testified that urine and other debris were nearly always present in the hallways and stairwells of the building. Further, plaintiff testified that while he did not see the urine before he slipped on it, he smelled it in the stairwell nearly two hours earlier.

In addition, a nonparty tenant testified that she saw urine on the steps in the location of plaintiffs fall 15 hours before the accident and again nearly five hours before the accident, at which time the condition of the steps had worsened, as even more urine and other debris were present.

She further testified that the porter rarely cleaned and did not adhere to a regular schedule, and that she and other tenants had complained to defendants about the dangerous condition of the stairwell, including a day or two before the accident, to no avail. She and another witness also testified that they had slipped on urine in the stairwell on multiple occasions.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal from the August 14, 2009 dismissal order as to Engineer’s Country Club.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted Engineer’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

facts.factual_summary: While playing golf on defendant’s golf course, plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell while descending stairs from the cart path to the eleventh tee box. The opinion does not identify a specific defect or substance causing the slip.

legal_issues.finding: Primary assumption of risk applied to this golf-course stairway accident, entitling Engineer’s to summary judgment under the rule covering inherent recreational risks.

quality.notes: Course ownership and personal slip mechanism are explicit, supporting inclusion despite the assumption-of-risk defense. Other injured role records golfer/recreational participant without assuming club membership or customer status. Specific hazard, accident date and evidence formats are not supplied. Open/obvious conditions appear in the general assumed-risk rule; no particular condition is identified or separately found obvious, so no independent obviousness holding is inferred. The whole limited appeal is affirmed; other parties or unappealed branches do not create additional orders. No specific stair defect is inferred from the staircase location.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

The plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell while playing golf on a golf course owned by the defendant Engineer’s Country Club, Inc. (hereinafter Engineer’s), when he descended a staircase leading from the cart path to the eleventh tee box.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals, as limited by his brief, from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Palmieri, J.), entered August 14, 2009, as granted the motion of the defendant Engineer’s Country Club, Inc., for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

Under the doctrine of primary assumption of the risk, “by engaging in a sport or recreational activity, a participant consents to those commonly appreciated risks which are inherent in and arise out of the nature of the sport generally and flow from such participation”
Those risks include risks associated with the construction of the playing surface and any open and obvious condition on it
Here, contrary to the plaintiffs contention, the doctrine of primary assumption of the risk applies
and thus, Engineer’s was entitled to summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.
